title: Step 1: Gathering Requirements & Scoping
tagline: The highest-ROI five minutes of the whole interview. Get this wrong and everything downstream is wrong.
summary: Functional vs non-functional requirements; the questions to ask.

paragraphs: You cannot design a system without knowing what it must do and how much load it must handle. Skipping this step is the single most common reason candidates fail — they design an elegant system for the wrong problem.
Interviewers deliberately give vague prompts to see if you'll narrow the scope yourself. Asking sharp clarifying questions is not a sign of weakness; it's the first thing they're grading.

blocks.title: You're scoping, not interrogating
blocks.text: Spend ~3–5 minutes. Ask focused questions, propose reasonable assumptions ('I'll assume we need photo upload and a feed, not video — sound good?'), and lock the scope. Don't ask 20 open questions; ask the few that change the design, then commit.

paragraphs: Functional requirements are the concrete features — the verbs of the system. Enumerate the core ones, then deliberately cut scope to the 2–4 that matter, deferring the rest.

items.detail: What are the main things a user does? (e.g., for a chat app: send/receive messages, see online status, group chats.)
End users? Internal services? Mobile vs web (affects offline/sync, connection handling)?
'Should I include search / notifications / analytics, or focus on the core read/write path?' Explicitly defer features to keep the design focused.

blocks.text: Write the agreed functional requirements in a corner of the whiteboard as a short list. It anchors the conversation and gives you something to revisit in the wrap-up ('we covered upload and feed; DMs were out of scope').

paragraphs: Non-functional requirements are where senior candidates shine. These are the system *qualities* — scale, speed, reliability — and they drive almost every architectural decision. This is where you decide what you're optimizing for.

items.detail: How many users / DAU? Reads vs writes ratio? This determines whether you even need distribution, caching, or sharding.
What's an acceptable response time? Is this user-facing (needs ms) or a background job (seconds/minutes ok)?
How bad is downtime? A payment system vs an internal dashboard have very different targets (and costs).
Is stale data acceptable for a few seconds (a like count) or never (an account balance)? This is the CAP/PACELC decision and it shapes your whole data layer.
Can you ever lose data? (A draft tweet vs a financial transaction.)

blocks.title: The framing that earns points
blocks.text: Don't list non-functional requirements neutrally — prioritize them and say so: 'This is read-heavy and user-facing, so I'll optimize for low read latency and high availability, and accept eventual consistency on counts.' Naming the trade-off you're choosing is exactly the senior signal interviewers look for.

paragraphs: One characterization shapes more of your design than any other: is the system read-heavy, write-heavy, or balanced? Establish it early — it's the lever for caching, replication, and data-store choices.

blocks.title: How the characterization drives design
rows: URL shortener, news feed, product catalog
Cache aggressively, read replicas, CDN, denormalize/precompute for reads
Buffer with queues, batch writes, LSM-tree stores (Cassandra), shard by write key
Strong consistency, transactions, careful concurrency control over raw speed

blocks.title: Don't skip estimation to 'get to the design'
blocks.text: The read/write ratio and rough QPS justify your decisions with numbers. Saying 'reads are 100× writes, so the cache is the centerpiece' is far stronger than asserting you'll cache without knowing why. Requirements and estimation are a package.

cheatsheet: Spend ~3–5 min: ask the few questions that change the design, propose assumptions, then lock scope.
Functional = the features (verbs). List the core ones; explicitly defer the rest to keep focus.
Non-functional = qualities: scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability.
Prioritize the non-functional requirements out loud — name what you're optimizing for and the trade-off.
Characterize read-heavy vs write-heavy vs consistency-critical — it drives caching, replication, and store choice.
Write the agreed requirements on the board; revisit them in the wrap-up.
Asking sharp clarifying questions is graded positively — it's not a sign of weakness.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between functional and non-functional requirements, and why do non-functional ones matter more for the architecture?
answer: Functional requirements describe *what the system does* — the concrete features and behaviors, like 'a user can post a photo' or 'a user can search messages'. They're the verbs. Non-functional requirements describe the *qualities* the system must have while doing those things: how much scale it handles, how fast it responds (latency), how available it is, how consistent the data needs to be, and how durable it is.

Non-functional requirements drive the architecture more because two systems with identical features can have radically different designs depending on their qualities. A photo app for 100 users is a single server and a database; the same features for 500M users read-heavy with low-latency feeds demands CDNs, caching, sharding, replication, and async fan-out. The features didn't change — the scale, latency, and availability targets did, and those dictate distribution, data stores, and consistency models. That's why strong candidates spend their clarifying time pinning down and *prioritizing* the non-functional requirements, then justify every later decision against them.
keyPoints: Same features + different scale/latency/availability = very different architecture
Non-functional requirements drive distribution, caching, data stores, consistency
Prioritize them and trace design decisions back to them
followUps: Give an example where a strict consistency requirement forces you to give up some availability.

questions.prompt: An interviewer gives you only 'Design a system to store and retrieve user files.' List the clarifying questions you'd ask before designing.
questions.hint: Cover both functional scope and non-functional scale/quality.
answer: I'd split my questions into functional and non-functional. Functional: What operations — just upload/download, or also sync across devices, sharing, versioning, search? What file types and size limits (a 10 KB text file vs a 4 GB video changes everything)? Single-user storage, or collaborative/shared access? Do we need offline access?

Non-functional: What's the scale — number of users, total storage, upload/download QPS? Is it read-heavy or write-heavy? What latency is acceptable for upload vs download? How critical is durability — can we ever lose a file (almost certainly not)? What availability target? Any consistency requirements when the same file is edited from two devices? Any geographic/compliance constraints (data residency)?

I'd then propose a scoped version — 'Let's focus on upload, download, and cross-device sync for files up to a few GB, optimizing for durability and bandwidth-efficient sync, and treat real-time collaborative editing as out of scope' — and confirm before designing. The point is to ask the handful of questions that genuinely change the design (size limits, sync, durability) rather than an exhaustive list.
keyPoints: Functional: operations, sync/share/version, file sizes/types, offline
Non-functional: scale/QPS, read vs write, latency, durability, availability, consistency
Surface constraints that change design (size, sync, durability, compliance)
Propose a scoped version and confirm before designing
followUps: How would a 4 GB max file size change your upload design versus a 1 MB limit?
